1:
Gill sets the chapter after the borders of the land were fixed, noting that the Levites, though holding no inheritance as a tribe, still needed cities, since they could not camp about the tabernacle for ever as they had in the wilderness. Calvin makes the same point from the other side, that the tithes compensated for want of land to sow and reap, but dwelling-places had still to be provided. Henry observes that no ground for tillage went with them, because the Levites were fed from the increase of other men's labours precisely so that they might study the law and have leisure to teach. That freedom was no indulgence, he insists, but release from the entangling affairs of this life, and the grouping into cities let them confer about the law to their mutual edification.

On why the tribe was scattered rather than settled together, Calvin gives the fullest answer, that the Levites were distributed over the whole land as guards regularly posted for the preservation of the worship of God, lest superstition creep in or the people fall into contempt of him. Had all been placed in one station, he argues, the law would soon have fallen into oblivion through the rest of the land, so their cities became schools, watchtowers, and lamps shining into the furthest corners. Both Calvin and Henry read the dispersion against Jacob's word that Levi would be scattered in Israel, and both take that curse to have been turned into a blessing. Ellicott states the purpose plainly, that the dispersion aimed primarily at the instruction of their brethren in the law, and suggests the Levites also discharged the functions now divided among the learned professions.

The measurements of the suburbs divide the commentators sharply, since verse four allows a thousand cubits from the wall and verse five two thousand on each side. Keil and Delitzsch read the second measure as a rule for laying out the lines, with the city standing in the middle and its own footprint not counted in the two thousand. Gill follows Jarchi and the Mishnah in adding the figures, the inner thousand for cattle and goods and the outer two thousand for fields and vineyards, while Wesley reaches three thousand by taking verse four to fix the space from which the measure begins and verse five the space to which it extends. Calvin rejects all such doubling as a subterfuge, holding that where Moses repeats himself the later verse only explains the earlier, and works out a geometrical reading in which the measure is taken round a circuit.

Clarke reports that the Septuagint and Coptic read two thousand in verse four as well, which would remove the difficulty, but concedes that no manuscript collated by Kennicott and De Rossi supports it, and falls back on Maimonides and a total of three thousand. Ellicott sets the common Jewish explanation beside that of Michaelis, who would add the length of the city wall, so that suburbs grew with the town, though he grants this accords less nearly with a measure fixed at two thousand in every case. On apportioning the forty-eight cities the sources agree, Keil and Delitzsch and Calvin alike taking the rule of much from the tribe that has much as plain equity, Calvin comparing it to assessing tribute by a man's means. For the six cities of refuge set among them Wesley gives three reasons, that the Levites would be impartial judges between manslayer and murderer, that their authority would bridle the pursuing avenger, and that they signified how sinners find refuge only in Christ, whom the Levitical priests represented.
9:
Calvin gives the cities a double purpose, to distinguish sins of malice from sins of error, and to keep innocent blood from being rashly shed and murder heaped on murder until the land was polluted. Keil and Delitzsch fix the number at six, three beyond Jordan and three in Canaan, and note that Deuteronomy has Moses tell the congregation to prepare the way and set a free city in each third of the land. Ellicott adds that Moses himself named Bezer, Ramoth in Gilead and Golan on the east, while the western three waited until the land was allotted in Joshua, and reckons no place stood above thirty miles from one. Calvin sees care in the siting, that the guiltless exile's banishment not be made bitter by distance, and Gill preserves the Jewish rules that such cities be of middling size, well watered and peopled, and sell no ropes or weapons lest the avenger come on pretence of buying.

Clarke marks off these cities sharply from the asyla of Greece and Rome and from the privileged altars of later use, which often sheltered the most profligate, whereas the Hebrew refuge protected only the man who had killed involuntarily. They were needed, he argues, because the patriarchal law that the nearest of kin avenge his relation's blood remained in force, and rash executions under it had to be qualified without being abolished. Ellicott explains the avenger as the goel, the near kinsman charged with redeeming his relative's person or inheritance and avenging his blood, and holds that this law checked his passions and secured a fair trial. Clarke and Wesley agree the refuge was temporary, a shelter until the elders examined publicly whether the killing was wilful or casual, and Gill cites the Targum for the same qualification, that the avenger acts once the court has condemned.

Calvin alone finds the arrangement troubling, saying it savours of barbarism that a private man be given the sword in his own cause, a very bad precedent that would let blood be added to blood. He resolves it by reading the licence as a danger denounced rather than a gate opened, since the fury of the bereaved could hardly be restrained, and vengeance on a true murderer went unpunished because it sprang from natural love of one's own blood. This, he insists, was tolerated and not approved, conceded to hardness of heart, since punishment belongs to public judgment and not to private will. Henry, less uneasy, gives the execution to the next of kin as naturally as the redemption of a mortgaged estate, but only where the fact was notorious, since suspicion could not empower him to do what the judges could not do without two witnesses.

On what marks a murderer, Henry lays down that wilful killing admits no sanctuary, no ransom and no commutation, whether by iron, wood, stone or the hand in enmity, and that blood defiles the land and is cleansed only by the murderer's blood. Calvin faces the apparent contradiction that God elsewhere absolves men who killed with iron or stone, answering that the instruments are named to foreclose subterfuge, since the will and not the outcome is punished. Keil and Delitzsch read a stone of the hand as one large enough to fill the hand and kill, Ellicott as a stone held in the hand whether thrown or wielded, while Wesley notes such a man dies even if he has reached the city. Both close on the stranger and the sojourner, whom Ellicott distinguishes as the passing foreigner and the settled resident, and whose common admission Henry reads as the figure that in Christ no difference is made between Greek and Jew.
22:
Gill takes the congregation for the court of judicature assembled to try the cause, and reads its deliverance of the slayer practically, as putting him in the care of proper persons to conduct him while the avenger is restrained until he arrives safely. Keil and Delitzsch insist the confinement was neither ordinary exile nor merely rescue from an enraged kinsman, but an appointment of the just and merciful God for the expiation of blood shed without intention. Wesley finds two ends served at once, that so severe a punishment for the mere appearance of murder shows how hateful the crime is to God, and that the manslayer's absence spares the kindred a provocation to fresh bloodshed.

Ellicott builds most on the term of the exile, arguing that since the anointing qualified the high priest to represent the nation and mediate on the day of atonement, his death took a representative character and typified that of the great High Priest. Clarke draws the figure more briefly, that no sinner is delivered from banishment or recovers his forfeited inheritance until Christ has died for his offences and risen for his justification, and Wesley reads that death as the only means whereby sins are pardoned. Calvin's reason is more human, that it would have been anything but kind to cut off all hope of restoration, and that a new priest succeeding to reconcile the people made a renewal of grace fit to propitiate offences of inadvertency. On the border, Keil and Delitzsch note that a slayer killed outside was not reckoned as blood, Wesley adding that the avenger was then not liable to punishment from men though not guiltless before God, while Ellicott makes the confinement a figure of exclusive reliance on Christ.

Calvin treats the rule of witnesses as the guard on the whole system, holding that none should be condemned unless lawfully convicted, and that it would be most unjust for a life to lie at the mercy of a single tongue. He and Clarke give the same practical reason, that two witnesses examined separately will scarcely accord in every particular, Clarke adding that one man may be mistaken, prejudiced, or malicious. Ellicott observes that the number is not specified here and supplies it from Deuteronomy, where two or three are required, and Calvin reads the ban on satisfaction as keeping the refuge from being purchasable.

Gill and Clarke agree that no ransom can save a murderer, Gill refusing all that a man's wealth or friends might offer, Clarke observing that civilised laws everywhere adjudge him to death or to a punishment differing only in being slower. Keil and Delitzsch state the principle plainly, that a land defiled by bloodshed has no expiation except the blood of the man who shed it, so that Israel would desecrate their own land by sparing the murderer. Calvin presses this as guilt before God rather than policy, since the stained land lies under a curse until expiation is made, and since God had chosen his abode among Israel his sanctity is profaned with it. Clarke adds a reason of his own, that God is the author of life and life the time to prepare for eternity, so one who cuts it short may murder a soul as well as a body, while Gill ends where the chapter does, on the Holy One dwelling among them as in no other land.
